The station is ten minutes on foot.

My colleague is helping me with it.

Auf der Zeichnung fehlt eine Maßangabe.

Ich muss mich beim Bürgeramt anmelden.
I have to register at the citizens' office.
We're applying for a residence permit.
Die Firma stellt zwei Ingenieure ein.
The company is hiring two engineers.
I handed in my notice for the end of the month.
We're developing a new drive system.
Can you explain that to me?
Ich freue mich auf den Umzug.
I'm looking forward to the move.
Ich kümmere mich um die Anmeldung.
I'll take care of the registration.

Die Grammatik ist am Anfang schwierig.
The grammar is difficult at the start.
I'll be finished in a moment.
Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich nach Deutschland ziehe.
I'm learning German because I'm moving to Germany.
Obwohl es schwer ist, macht es Spaß.
Es regnet, deshalb bleiben wir zu Hause.

Es war spät, trotzdem habe ich weitergelernt.
It was late, nevertheless I kept studying.
Sobald ich ankomme, melde ich mich.
As soon as I arrive, I'll get in touch.
Ich übe täglich, damit ich schneller lerne.
I practise daily so that I learn faster.

I've been learning German for three months.

Besides, I still need an appointment.
Während der Besprechung war es sehr laut.

items.en: Excuse me, I have a question.
What does that mean in German?
That's beyond me / I've no idea.
I'll take a look at it.
Where do I find the entrance?

s: Ich fahre mit ___ Bus zur Arbeit.
I take the bus to work.

items.en: in takes the accusative for movement
auf takes the dative for position
s: The tool is lying on the table.
I thank you for the help.
Der Zug ist ___ als das Auto.
The train is faster than the car.
Ich arbeite ___ einer Firma in München.
I work at a company in Munich.
The robot consists of many components.
Ich bewerbe mich ___ eine Stelle als Ingenieur.
I'm applying for a position as an engineer.
On Monday I have an appointment.

items.en: modal verb sends the infinitive to the end
s: Ich muss heute noch die Messung ___.
I still have to do the measurement today.
Nächstes Jahr ziehe ich nach Deutschland.
Next year I'm moving to Germany.
Ich arbeite vier Tage pro Woche.
I work four days a week.
In the evening I like to read.
Am Morgen trinke ich immer Kaffee.
In the morning I always drink coffee.
Um wie viel Uhr fängt der Film an?
What time does the film start?
What are you doing at the weekend?
Sie ist ein sehr offener Mensch.
The child is playing in the garden.
Der Chef ist heute nicht da.
Die Stadt ist im Sommer voller Touristen.
The city is full of tourists in summer.
Kannst du mir den Weg zeigen?
Can you show me the way?
Wir wohnen in einer ruhigen Straße.
We live on a quiet street.
Mein Auto ist in der Werkstatt.
My car is at the garage.
Der Zug hat zwanzig Minuten Verspätung.
The train is twenty minutes late.
Wegen der Verspätung komme ich zu spät.
Because of the delay I'll be late.
Ich kaufe die Fahrkarte am Automaten.
I'm buying the ticket at the machine.
How do I get to the airport?
Im Urlaub fahre ich ans Meer.
On holiday I'm going to the seaside.
I don't have any money on me.
Ich warte noch auf eine Antwort.
I'm still waiting for an answer.
Do you have a better idea?
I have to go to the doctor's tomorrow.
Health is the most important thing.
Es gibt noch eine andere Möglichkeit.
Die Aufgabe ist schwerer als gedacht.
The task is harder than I thought.
Mein Ziel ist es, fließend Deutsch zu sprechen.
My goal is to speak German fluently.
Das Ergebnis ist besser als erwartet.
The result is better than expected.
Das Gemüse vom Markt ist frischer.
The vegetables from the market are fresher.
Die Küche ist klein, aber praktisch.
The kitchen is small but practical.
Mein Zimmer ist im ersten Stock.
My room is on the first floor.
The plates are in the cupboard.
Can you see that sign there?
Gibst du mir bitte das Salz?
Can you pass me the salt, please?
What do you think of the flat?
Do you know a good restaurant?
Ich lese jeden Abend im Bett.
I read in bed every evening.
What are you having for lunch?
Do you drink tea or coffee?
Er fährt jeden Tag mit dem Rad zur Arbeit.
He cycles to work every day.
Ich laufe jeden Morgen fünf Kilometer.
I run five kilometres every morning.
Ich lerne jeden Tag zehn neue Wörter.
I learn ten new words every day.
I'm just quickly buying some bread.
I'm looking for a new job.
Er antwortet nie auf meine E-Mails.
He never replies to my emails.
I've been waiting for ten minutes.
Ich stehe um sechs Uhr auf.
I get up at six o'clock.
On Saturday I do the shopping.
Ich bereite mich auf das Gespräch vor.
I want to become an engineer.
I practise the piano every day.
I want to improve my German.
Erzähl mal, wie war der Urlaub?
Tell me, how was the holiday?

items.en: to be right, to be true

s: Die Wohnung ist groß und hell.
The flat is big and bright.
Das Zimmer ist leider sehr klein.
Unfortunately the room is very small.
Das Haus ist über hundert Jahre alt.
The house is over a hundred years old.
Du sprichst zu schnell für mich.
You're speaking too fast for me.
Sei bitte leise, das Baby schläft.
Please be quiet, the baby's asleep.
The train is on time today.
Im Winter ist es hier sehr kalt.
It's very cold here in winter.
Ich bin gerade in der Bahn.
I'm on the train right now.
I never drink coffee in the evening.
Wie oft gehst du ins Fitnessstudio?
How often do you go to the gym?
Sometimes I cook at the weekend.
Beeil dich, sonst verpassen wir den Zug.
Hurry up, otherwise we'll miss the train.

items.en: on the way, out and about

s: By the way, tomorrow is a public holiday.
That's just the way it is.
After that I'm going to bed.
I hope that it works out.
Wenn ich Zeit habe, rufe ich dich an.
If I have time, I'll call you.
Do you know if he's coming?

items.en: when (once, in the past; verb goes last)
s: Als ich klein war, hatte ich einen Hund.
When I was little, I had a dog.
Ich nehme einen Schirm mit, denn es regnet.
I'm taking an umbrella, because it's raining.
Das ist nicht rot, sondern blau.
Erst essen wir, dann gehen wir spazieren.
First we eat, then we go for a walk.

items.en: I don't mind. / I don't care.

items.de: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?
items.en: How do you say that in German?
I'll keep my fingers crossed for you.
That's not my problem. (idiom: not my beer)

items.de: Hast du Tomaten auf den Augen?
items.en: Are you blind?! (idiom: tomatoes on your eyes)
Let's talk on the phone tomorrow.

items.why: Verb second. 'Heute' takes the first spot, so the verb comes next. Then 'ich'.

items.de: Morgen | *fahre | ich | mit dem Zug | nach Berlin.
items.en: Tomorrow I'm taking the train to Berlin.
items.why: Verb second, then the person. After that: how (mit dem Zug), then where to (nach Berlin).

items.de: Ich | *fahre | morgen | mit dem Zug | nach Berlin.
items.en: I'm going to Berlin by train tomorrow.
items.why: Order after the verb: when, then how, then where. Morgen, then mit dem Zug, then nach Berlin.
Yes/no question: the verb goes first.

items.en: When does the meeting start tomorrow?
items.why: W-question: the question word first, the verb second.

items.en: I have to work late today.
items.why: The modal verb (muss) goes in position 2. The other verb goes to the very end.
Question with a modal verb: the modal goes first, the main verb goes last.

items.en: We want to move to Munich in the summer.
items.why: wollen goes in position 2. ziehen goes to the end.
Past (Perfekt): haben goes in position 2. The past form (gestellt) goes at the end.

items.en: We went to Hamburg at the weekend.
items.why: Movement verbs use sein. sein goes in position 2. gefahren goes at the end.

items.en: The train arrives at eight o'clock.
items.why: ankommen is a separable verb. The 'an' breaks off and goes to the end.
anrufen splits. rufe goes in position 2. an goes to the end. A short word like dich comes early.
A command starts with the verb. zumachen splits, so zu goes to the end.

items.de: Ich | *lerne | Deutsch, | weil | ich | bald | nach Deutschland | *ziehe.
items.en: I'm learning German because I'm moving to Germany soon.
items.why: weil sends the verb to the very end of its part of the sentence.

items.de: Ich | *bleibe | heute | zu Hause, | weil | ich | krank | *bin.
items.en: I'm staying at home today because I'm ill.
items.why: After weil, the verb (bin) goes last.

items.en: I think the sensor is broken.
items.why: dass sends the verb to the end.

items.en: I don't know whether he's coming today.
items.why: ob (whether) works like dass: the verb goes to the end.

items.en: If I have time, I'll come along.
items.why: The wenn part ends with its verb (habe). Then the main part starts with its verb (komme).

items.en: Although it's raining, we're going for a walk.
items.why: The verb goes last in the obwohl part. That whole part counts as position 1, so the next verb (gehen) comes straight after the comma.

items.en: I'm tired, but I still have to study.
items.why: aber does not change the word order. After aber it's a normal sentence: verb second.

items.en: It's raining, so we're staying at home.
items.why: deshalb takes position 1, so the verb comes straight after it. aber doesn't do this, deshalb does.

items.de: Ich | *war | müde, | trotzdem | *habe | ich | noch eine Stunde | *gelernt.
items.en: I was tired, but I still studied for another hour.
items.why: trotzdem takes position 1, so the verb comes next. Past (Perfekt): gelernt goes at the end.
With one simple verb, nicht usually goes near the end. It comes after time words like heute.
nicht goes just before the past form at the end (verstanden).

items.en: I'm giving the colleague the tool.
items.why: Two nouns: the person who gets it (dative) comes before the thing (accusative).
Two pronouns: the thing (es) comes before the person (ihm). That's the opposite of nouns!
A pronoun comes before a noun. So ihm comes before das Werkzeug.

items.de: Ich | *freue | mich | sehr | auf das Wochenende.
items.en: I'm really looking forward to the weekend.
items.why: The reflexive word (mich) comes straight after the verb.
alt: Auf das Wochenende | *freue | ich | mich | sehr.

items.why: Future: werden goes in position 2, the other verb at the end. Here anrufen stays in one piece.

items.de: Das | *ist | der Kollege, | der | mir | immer | *hilft.
items.en: That's the colleague who always helps me.
items.why: In a 'who/which' part (der = who), the verb goes to the end.

items.de: Es | *ist | wichtig, | jeden Tag | ein bisschen | *zu üben.
items.en: It's important to practise a little every day.
items.why: zu + verb goes at the very end.
alt: Es | *ist | wichtig, | ein bisschen | jeden Tag | *zu üben.

items.de: Ich | *lerne | Deutsch, | um | in Deutschland | *zu arbeiten.
items.en: I'm learning German so that I can work in Germany.
items.why: um … zu means 'in order to'. um starts that part. zu + verb ends it.

items.en: Do you know when the train is coming?
items.why: Hidden question: after wann, the verb (kommt) goes to the end.
kann goes in position 2, kommen at the end. nicht goes just before kommen.

items.en: I get up at seven every day.
items.why: aufstehen splits. stehe goes in position 2. auf goes to the end.

items.en: I know that I have to get up early.
items.why: In a dass part, the modal (muss) goes last, after the other verb. And aufstehen joins back into one word.

items.de: Er | *sagt, | dass | er | den Bericht | schon | *geschickt | *hat.
items.en: He says that he has already sent the report.
items.why: Past after dass: the past form (geschickt) comes first, then hat at the very end.
alt: Er | *sagt, | dass | er | schon | den Bericht | *geschickt | *hat.

items.why: Yes/no question: the verb first. Sie (polite 'you') comes right after.

items.en: I've been learning German for three months.
items.why: Even a long time phrase counts as position 1. The verb comes next.

items.de: Als | ich | ein Kind | *war, | *wollte | ich | Ingenieur | *werden.
items.en: When I was a child, I wanted to be an engineer.
items.why: als (when, in the past) sends war to the end. Then the main part starts with its verb (wollte).
With one simple verb, nicht often goes right at the end.

items.de: Am Montag | *fange | ich | bei der neuen Firma | *an.
items.en: On Monday I start at the new company.
items.why: Verb second after 'Am Montag'. anfangen splits, so an goes to the end.

items.de: Ich | *gehe | früh | ins Bett, | denn | ich | *bin | müde.
items.en: I'm going to bed early, because I'm tired.
items.why: denn also means 'because', but it does NOT move the verb. Compare weil, which sends it to the end.
sehen takes the accusative. Only masculine words change: der becomes den.
The bus is doing the action, so it's nominative: der.

items.en: I have an appointment at the doctor's.
items.why: haben takes the accusative. der Termin becomes einen Termin.
die Wohnung is feminine. In the accusative it stays eine.
der Hunger, accusative: keinen. kein works just like ein.
der Schlüssel, accusative: meinen. mein has the same endings as ein.

items.de: Ich fahre mit ___ Fahrrad zur Arbeit.
items.why: mit always takes the dative. das Fahrrad becomes dem Fahrrad.

items.de: Nach ___ Arbeit gehe ich ins Fitnessstudio.
items.en: After work I go to the gym.
items.why: nach always takes the dative. die Arbeit becomes der Arbeit.

items.en: We've known each other for a year.
items.why: seit always takes the dative. ein Jahr becomes einem Jahr.

items.de: Ich bekomme eine E-Mail von ___ Chefin.
items.en: I'm getting an email from the boss (she).
items.why: von always takes the dative. die Chefin becomes der Chefin.

items.en: The present is for the boss.
items.why: für always takes the accusative. der Chef becomes den Chef.

items.en: It won't work without my ID.
items.why: ohne always takes the accusative. der Ausweis becomes meinen Ausweis.
durch always takes the accusative. der Park becomes den Park.

items.de: Ich stelle die Lampe neben ___ Fernseher.
items.en: I'm putting the lamp next to the TV.
items.why: stellen means you move it somewhere (wohin?). Movement takes the accusative: den.

items.en: The lamp is next to the TV.
items.why: stehen means it's already there (wo?). No movement takes the dative: dem.

items.de: Ich hänge das Bild an ___ Wand.
items.en: I'm hanging the picture on the wall.
items.why: Movement (wohin?) takes the accusative. die Wand stays die.

items.en: The picture is hanging on the wall.
items.why: No movement (wo?) takes the dative. die Wand becomes der Wand.

items.en: I'm going to the cinema today.
items.why: Going into somewhere takes the accusative. in + das = ins.
Being somewhere (wo?) takes the dative. in + dem = im.
zu takes the dative. der Bahnhof becomes dem Bahnhof. zu + dem = zum.

items.en: I still have to go to the post office.
items.why: zu takes the dative. die Post becomes der Post. zu + der = zur.

items.en: I was at the doctor's yesterday.
items.why: bei means at someone's place. bei + dem = beim. You go zum Arzt, but you are beim Arzt.
anrufen takes the accusative: mich.

items.en: Can you pass me the salt?
items.why: The person who gets something is dative: mir.
gefallen takes the dative. German says 'the flat pleases us'.
gehören takes the dative: dir.
kennen takes the accusative. er becomes ihn.
antworten takes the dative. sie (her) becomes ihr.
schmecken takes the dative: ihm.
The genitive shows who owns it: des. der Nachbar becomes des Nachbarn.

items.de: Wegen ___ Wetters bleiben wir zu Hause.
items.en: Because of the weather, we're staying at home.
items.why: wegen takes the genitive. das Wetter becomes des Wetters (with an extra -s).

items.en: During the week I work a lot.
items.why: während takes the genitive. die Woche becomes der Woche.
Dative plural: the noun gets an extra -n. die Kinder becomes den Kindern.
helfen takes the dative. die Nachbarin becomes der Nachbarin.
es geht takes the dative. Wie geht es dir?
There's already a thing being washed (die Hände). So the 'myself' word becomes dative: mir.

items.de: Der Arzt gibt ___ Patienten ein Rezept.
items.en: The doctor gives the patient a prescription.
items.why: The patient gets something, so it's dative. der Patient becomes dem Patienten.

items.en: I'm looking forward to the holiday.
items.why: sich freuen auf takes the accusative. der Urlaub becomes den Urlaub.

items.en: The new colleague is very nice.
items.why: After der, die or das (nominative), the adjective ends in -e.

items.de: Ich kenne den ___ Kollegen noch nicht.
items.en: I don't know the new colleague yet.
items.why: After den (accusative), the ending is -en.
ein doesn't show the gender, so the adjective does. der Plan, so -er.
ein doesn't show the gender, so the adjective does. das Problem, so -es.
eine + a feminine word: -e.

items.en: I'm looking for a good job.
items.why: einen (accusative, masculine): -en.
In the dative, after dem, der or einem, the ending is always -en.

items.en: She lives in a small town.
items.why: Dative (einer): the ending is -en.
Plural with die: -en.
No article, so the adjective takes the ending den would have: -en.
No article, so the adjective takes the ending das would have: -es.
No article. das Brot, so the adjective ends in -es.
eine + a feminine word: -e.

items.en: Kind regards (end of a formal email)
items.why: mit takes the dative. Plural, no article: -en. You'll write this at the end of every formal email.
Plural with no article: -e.

items.en: My older brother lives in Cologne.
items.why: mein works like ein. der Bruder, nominative: -er.
